meaning: Greek neuter of εἷς, "one"; philosophically "The One" in Neoplatonism.

phonemes.desc: Rough breathing [h], the audible breath that precedes the vowel in classical Greek.
Short epsilon with acute pitch stress [ɛ́], the prosodic peak of the word.
Voiced alveolar nasal [n], closing the syllable.

pronunciation.approximation: 'HEN' — with a slight initial h and a rising pitch on the first, only syllable.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: τὸ ἕν (to hen), 'the one' — the neuter form used in philosophical texts

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἑνάς (henás), 'unit, monad' — the later philosophical noun derived from the numeral

kin.label: PIE

pronunciation.note: Hén is Tier 2: the Greek ἕν carries the acute pitch accent on a short initial vowel but no long vowel (η/ω) and no circumflex, so exactly one Tier-1 feature survives. It is an Accent-Preserving Tier-2 name.

domains.title: The One
domains.subtitle: Unity, First Principle, and Indivisibility
domains.lead: Hén is the Greek neuter of εἷς, 'one'. In everyday speech it is simply the number; in philosophy it became one of the most powerful words in the Western tradition. For Parmenides, Plato, and the Neoplatonists, τὸ ἕν names the ultimate source from which all multiplicity flows.

cards.name: Unity
cards.desc: The indivisible whole that precedes every plurality and every distinction.

cards.name: The Good
cards.desc: In Plato, the first principle beyond being is identified with the Form of the Good, source of all knowability (Republic 509b).

cards.name: First Principle
cards.desc: For Plotinus, τὸ ἕν is the first hypostasis, absolutely simple and unknowable, from which Mind and Soul proceed (Enneads V.1).

cards.name: Indivisibility
cards.desc: What is truly one cannot be divided without ceasing to be itself; it is the root of identity.

symbols.name: Circle
symbols.meaning: The perfect shape without parts or beginning, symbol of unity.

symbols.name: Point
symbols.meaning: A geometric entity with no magnitude, the mathematical image of the One.

symbols.name: Monad
symbols.meaning: The Pythagorean unit from which the number series and cosmos arise.

symbols.name: Radiant centre
symbols.meaning: The source from which all lines and all beings emanate.

mythology.lead: Hén has no myths in the usual sense, because it is not a person but a principle — yet its philosophical biography is one of the great narratives of ancient thought. From Pythagorean counting to Eleatic logic, from Plato's sun to Plotinus's mystical return, the tiny word gathers the whole destiny of Greek metaphysics.

myths.title: What Is Is One
myths.text: Around 475 BCE a citizen of Elea carried his poem On Nature through the Greek world, reporting a revelation: brought by mares and the daughters of the Sun past the gates of Night and Day, he was received by a goddess who taught him 'the unshaken heart of well-rounded truth' (frag. 1). Her doctrine is the austerity itself of thought: 'is, and it is impossible for it not to be' (frag. 2). What genuinely is must be one — whole, unique, motionless, without beginning or end (frag. 8). Change, plurality, and coming-to-be belong to the 'way of mortal opinion', the second half of the poem, recited only so it may be named and dismissed. Nothing in earlier Greek literature argues this hard. The One enters philosophy not as a mystic blur but as a logical cage: deny it, and your own words betray you, for to speak of what-is-not is to speak of nothing.

myths.title: The One and the Good
myths.text: Plato gave the One its most influential passage without quite naming it. In the Republic (509b), Socrates calls the Form of the Good 'beyond being in dignity and power' — the source that makes all other forms knowable, as the sun makes things visible. Later Platonists fused sun and syllable: the Good simply is to hen. The dialogue Parmenides then ran the experiment in reverse, asking what follows if the One is, and again if the One is not (137c–166c): in the first hypothesis the One cannot even partake of being, since partaking would divide it. Some ancients dismissed the exercise as logical gymnastic; the Neoplatonists read it as the via negativa written in Plato's own hand. Either way, the identification of unity with goodness became the hinge of Western metaphysics: whatever is most real is most simple, and whatever is most simple is most good.

myths.title: The One beyond Intellect
myths.text: Plotinus (204/5–270 CE), teaching in Rome, made to hen the first of three hypostases: the One, Intellect (Nous), and Soul (Enneads V.1). The One is beyond being, beyond thought, beyond even self-awareness — for awareness implies duality, and duality is the first fall. From it Intellect proceeds eternally, thinking the forms it contains; from Intellect proceeds Soul, which orders the material cosmos and, in us, turns back toward its source (V.4). The return is the point: every hypostasis flows out of the One and aspires back, like light indifferent to distance. Plotinus claimed firsthand acquaintance with it — 'four times in the years of my life' (Porphyry, Vita Plotini 23). Philosophy here completes the trajectory the goddess of Elea began: the One that Parmenides proved and Plato glimpsed becomes an addressable presence, the terminus of the soul's one true eros.

myths.title: The Monad
myths.text: Earlier than both, and stranger, stood the Pythagoreans, who did not argue for the One but counted with it. Aristotle reports their founding thesis: the elements of number are the elements of all things, and the whole heaven is harmony and number (Metaphysics 986a). Their first principle was the monad — the unit, to hen by another name — from which the dyad, the number series, and finally the cosmos unfolded; their oath swore by the tetraktys, the holy triangle of ten that holds 'the fount and root of ever-flowing nature'. Number was not description but substance: justice was four, marriage five, opportunity seven. Later tradition credits Pythagoras with calling the one both even and odd (Aristotle, Physics 203a). Where Elea reached unity by stripping away, Pythagoras reached it by building up — one dot, then two, then the world. Greek mathematics, and with it Greek science, begins in this religious arithmetic of the ἕν.

lore.syncretism: The Greek ἕν shaped Jewish and Christian monotheism through Philo and the Church Fathers, who read the biblical God through Platonist categories — Augustine's Trinity leans directly on Plotinus, and Aquinas argues that God, as ipsum esse, is supremely one. In Indian philosophy, the Upaniṣadic Brahman offers an analogous reflection on unity beyond plurality, though the two traditions reached it by different roads. The modern mathematical unit and the philosophical problem of the one and the many both descend from this small Greek word: set theory's generator, Spinoza's substance, and the recurring mystical claim that all things are one are footnotes to the dialectic begun at Elea.
lore.culturalLegacy: From the Pythagorean monad to Neoplatonic mysticism, from Spinoza's substance to the unit element of modern algebra, the One has never ceased to shape Western thought. In mathematics the number 1 became the generator of the whole series; in set theory, the empty set's successor. The mystics made it devotional — the 'One' of Eckhart and of the Sufi waḥdat al-wujūd is the same word translated across three faiths. Restoring Hén in Unicode preserves the acute accent that marks the word's classical pitch: a single diacritic carrying an entire metaphysical lineage, the smallest possible monument to the largest possible claim.
lore.extendedMeditation: The smallest entry in this lexicon carries the largest claim. Hén is one syllable, one breath, one phoneme-cluster of Greek — and it names what all syllables, breaths, and Greeks were thought to come from. The name teaches a lesson in scale: in the Greek imagination, ultimate reality is not a bigger thing but a simpler one; not a universe packed with content but a unity from which content can proceed without diminishing it. That is why the tradition never outgrew the word. Philosophers could complicate the architecture — hypostases, emanations, triads — but the roof stayed the same. To restore the accent on Hén is to keep the pitch of that roof: a word whose entire office is to be indivisible, marked by the only stress it can bear.

lore.archaeology: No cult or temple attaches to Hén, but the word is among the best-traveled survivors of ancient thought. Parmenides' poem reaches us through quotations in Simplicius's sixth-century commentaries; Plato's dialogues and Plotinus's Enneads descend through the medieval manuscript tradition — the Plato of Constantinople and the Plotinus of the Arabic translators of Baghdad. In papyri and school exercises the word appears endlessly, glossed for generations of students as the first of the numbers and the root of henology. Its material biography is therefore the biography of Greek literacy itself: a one-syllable word that had to be copied, century after century, because everything else depended on it.
